common_misconceptions.topic: Lesser vs greater Jihad in Islam
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students often reduce Jihad to 'holy war' or oversimplify the greater/lesser distinction as 'inner struggle vs holy war'. Greater Jihad is the spiritual struggle against the lower self (nafs); lesser Jihad is defensive struggle in specific conditions (e.g. Surah 2:190-194). The conditions for declaration of lesser Jihad are tightly constrained in classical Islamic jurisprudence.
common_misconceptions.source: NATRE research on teaching about Islam (Picturing Islam, Picturing Muslims project, RE Today/NATRE) — teachers' confidence in teaching Islam is uneven and 'theology vs everyday lived Islam' is a frequent gap.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate Aquinas's First Three Ways (motion, causation, contingency) with the Ontological Argument or with the Kalam Cosmological Argument. They are distinct: Aquinas's first three ways are a posteriori arguments from features of the world; the Ontological Argument (Anselm) is a priori and not in Edexcel 1RA0 Paper 3; Kalam (al-Ghazali) is the Islamic version in Paper 3C.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel 1RA0 specification — Aquinas First Three Ways named explicitly in 3A 1.6 and 3B 1.7; Kalam in 3C 1.6 with al-Ghazali named.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse Augustine's free-will defence (evil as the privation of good, caused by misuse of free will, the Fall) with Irenaean soul-making (evil as a necessary feature for moral and spiritual development, developed in the modern era by John Hick). Both are Edexcel-named in 3A 1.8 and feed into 1B 1.8 problem-of-evil content.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel 1RA0 spec, 3A 1.8 names St Augustine and St Irenaeus by name.

common_misconceptions.topic: Catholic vs general Christian framing in Paper 3
common_misconceptions.misconception: Paper 3A students writing on the Paper 3B (general Christianity) framing or vice versa. The Catholic paper (3A) requires references to Catechism paragraphs, papal documents (Humanae Vitae, Familiaris Consortio, Evangelii Gaudium, Not Just Good But Beautiful) and Magisterium teaching specifically. 3B Christianity is denomination-wide.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson 1RA0 spec — 3A explicitly references Catechism numbers throughout; 3B does not.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students cite the 'longer ending' (Mark 16:9-20) as the canonical resurrection account in Mark. The spec specifies Mark 16:1-8 (the empty tomb, women fleeing in fear). The longer ending is widely considered a later addition by textual scholars.

Students claim Islam denies Jesus existed, or that Muslims believe Jesus was a mere prophet 'like any other'. Islam affirms Isa as one of the greatest prophets, born of a virgin mother through divine intervention, the Messiah, and raised to heaven by Allah before the crucifixion (Surah 4:157-158 reads 'they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them'). This is a respectful theological position, not a denial of Christianity.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson 1RA0 spec, 4B 2.7 explicitly references Surah 4:157-158 on Isa's death; NATRE guidance on teaching Islam respectfully.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sources of authority in 5-mark Explain questions
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students get the 5-mark Explain question (which requires one source of wisdom or authority) wrong by either omitting the source citation altogether, paraphrasing without attribution, or citing a source that doesn't actually say what they claim. Examiners flag this consistently — the source must be named (e.g. 'In Surah 2:183', 'In Catechism 2360', 'In the Lord's Prayer') and used to support the explanation, not decorate it.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel exemplar answer packs (2024 series, both Christianity and Catholic Christianity); Pearson Religious Studies subject updates discuss the 5-mark source-of-wisdom requirement repeatedly.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students develop their own view in depth on a 12-mark Discuss but treat the 'other side' as a single brief sentence ('Christians might disagree because...') with no scriptural anchor or reasoning. Examiners consistently note that the alternative perspective is the weakest point of student responses — it must be developed with the same depth as the main argument and supported by a named source where possible.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel 2024 exemplar answer commentary — 'alternative points of view being brief rather than fully developed and development being more descriptive than explanatory' (qualifications.pearson.com 2024 exemplar packs).

student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Outline Three: Students give one extended answer instead of three discrete points. Each of the three must be a separate identifiable point — not three sentences elaborating one idea. Examiners credit the first three discrete points only.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain Two: Students give two points but only briefly state each — no development. 'Explain' demands development 'beyond a habitual response' (Edexcel command-word definition). Two well-developed points beats four undeveloped ones.
student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — Explain Two with Sources: Students offer two points but only one source, or no clear source, or a vague paraphrase 'the Bible says we should love our neighbour' without naming a specific reference. The 5th mark depends on the source being identifiable (book, surah, named teaching, named Catechism paragraph, named hadith).
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Discuss a Statement: Three common failure modes: (1) the alternative point of view is underdeveloped, (2) the conclusion restates rather than evaluates, (3) the argument relies on opinion without scriptural or doctrinal backing. The best 12-mark answers present 2-3 developed reasons on each side, weigh them explicitly, and reach a justified judgement. SPaG marks are additional (3 marks on selected questions) — students often forget terminology that earns SPaG.

topic_weighting_notes: Paper 1 (50%) is twice the weighting of any other single paper. Beliefs and Practices content is heavily examined; Sources of Wisdom and Forms of Expression sections sometimes appear as the 5-mark or 12-mark questions in Paper 1 question (c) or (d). Don't shortchange those sections.

Within each Paper 1/2 religion, the comparison-marked spec points (1.x* and 2.x* — e.g. Catholic 1.8 eschatology, 2.2 liturgical worship) consistently anchor the 12-mark Discuss questions because they explicitly require comparison with another tradition.

Paper 4 (Textual Studies) is the unfamiliar option for most students — fewer schools teach it than Paper 3 (Philosophy & Ethics). Make Paper 4 content welcoming and explicit about the named passages, because students will rely heavily on these lessons.

Pope Francis (Not Just Good But Beautiful, Evangelii Gaudium), Humanae Vitae (Paul VI), Familiaris Consortio (John Paul II) are the Edexcel-named papal documents — Catholic students must know what each one teaches and which pope wrote it.
Surah anchors and Catechism paragraph numbers appear repeatedly in 5-mark Explain questions because they fulfil the 'named source' requirement. Build them into key-facts boxes.
current_spec_changes: Edexcel 1RA0 Issue 2 (January 2024): topic references (e.g. 1A, 1B) and section names added throughout the spec; the definition of 'evaluate' in the command-word taxonomy was updated to align better with the updated 2024 mark schemes. Mark schemes were amended; first assessment under amended level descriptors was Summer 2024. Source: Pearson Edexcel 1RA0 specification Issue 2, page 1 ('Summary of changes').
pedagogical_notes: EEF research on retrieval practice (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk): retrieval of incorrect information embeds misconceptions, so feedback must address misconceptions before adding new material. For RS, this means the knowledge-check questions must surface and explicitly correct common factual errors (wrong scripture cited, wrong attribution of theological position, conflated denominational stance), not just test recall.

EEF guidance on diagnostic assessment: anticipate likely misconceptions and use diagnostic probes early in a topic. For RS this maps onto the 'common misconceptions' list above — each one should be a deliberate prompt in either a key-fact, a knowledge check, or a glossary term, not a one-off correction.

NATRE guidance on teaching about Islam: 25% of UK teachers report low confidence teaching Islam. Avoid 'textbook Islam' that focuses purely on doctrine — show lived practice, diversity within Sunni/Shi'a/Sufi, and avoid stereotype-reinforcing imagery (the 'Picturing Islam' resource shows the diversity problem clearly).

RE Today / NATRE: comparison and contrast skills benefit from explicit scaffolding — Venn diagrams, paired-paragraph writing with model amendment. For Edexcel's 12-mark Discuss this maps directly: students need a structural template for handling the comparison side of the argument.

Theos Think Tank (theosthinktank.co.uk): the shift from 'theological' to 'sociological' framing in RE has trade-offs — students can lose sight of religion as a normative framework. For Edexcel RS, this means presenting beliefs as believers hold them, not just describing them externally. Maintain DfE political-impartiality guidance throughout — present divergent positions fairly without endorsing.

Pearson Edexcel 2024 exemplar packs (Christianity and Catholic Christianity): the strongest 12-mark answers do three things — develop both sides with named sources, weigh them explicitly using evaluative connectives, and close with a justified conclusion that picks a side. The weakest ones list points without weighing, leave the alternative view as a one-line concession, or conclude with 'it is a matter of personal opinion'.

batch_teaching_note: Paper 2 Abrahamic second-religion units (4 lessons each = 12 total). These reuse Paper 1 content but compressed — no Sources/Forms sections. Frame the intro for students whose main religion is a different tradition (e.g. a student taking Islam as Paper 1 now studying Catholic Christianity as Paper 2). All content_transfer scores are HIGH — refer to _aqa_source_lessons.json. Starred spec points: 2A 1.8*, 2A 2.2*, 2B 1.6*, 2B 2.1*, 2C 1.8*, 2C 2.3*.
